'''Andrew Eben Strominger''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|t|r|ɒ|m|ɪ|n|dʒ|ər}}; born July 30, 1955) is an American [[theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] who is the director of Harvard's [[Center for the Fundamental Laws of Nature]]. He specializes in [[quantum gravity]] and [[string theory]] who is known for early work on [[celestial holography]]. He co-formulated the [[SYZ conjecture]] and the [[CGHS model]]. 

Strominger won the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] in 2017. He was elected as a fellow to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2001, to the [[American Physical Society]] in 2018, and as a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]] in 2020.

==Education and early life==
Strominger was born in [[Cambridge, England]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Strominger, Andrew Eben |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11609043.html |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref> to Jewish father [[Jack L. Strominger|Jack Strominger]], a [[biochemist]], and Ann,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mineo |first=Liz |date=2020-01-06 |title=Jack Strominger to retire after a lifetime of achievement |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2020/01/jack-strominger-to-retire-after-a-lifetime-of-achievement/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Harvard Gazette |language=en-US}}</ref> who had grown up on a [[Family farm|farm]] in [[Minnesota]] as a [[Catholic Church|Catholic]]. Before Strominger's first birthday, the family moved to [[St. Louis|St. Louis, Missouri]], where his father was an [[assistant professor]] at [[Washington University in St. Louis|Washington University]]. Six years later, his father was offered a chair at [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin]] in [[Madison, Wisconsin]]; where they lived until he was 13. He spent the rest of his childhood in [[Lexington, Massachusetts]], with three brothers, where his father was a professor at [[Harvard University]]. He said he and his brothers were interested in science and spent time in their father's labs.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Zierler |first=David |date=September 16, 2020 |title=Strominger, Andrew on 2020 September 16. |url=https://repository.aip.org/node/129377 |website=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> He attended [[The Cambridge School of Weston]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-09-19 |title=Gryphon: Spring/Summer 2017 |url=https://issuu.com/wearecsw/docs/139067_spc_gryphon_final_2/34 |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Issuu |language=en}}</ref>{{efn|The source lists Strominger as the class of 1972, but he stopped attending in 1970.}} but after reading ''[[The Feynman Lectures on Physics]]'', he decided he was "done with high school," describing himself as a troubled teen who got involved in [[substance abuse]]. He stopped attending in 1970<ref name=":1" /> when he was a [[sophomore]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |title=The Gryphon |publisher=The Cambridge School of Weston |year=1970 |location=Weston, MA |pages=20}}</ref> 

At age 15, Strominger left home and moved to [[New Hampshire]] to live in a [[Intentional community|commune]],<ref name=":1" /> until he was 18.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-10-06 |title=How Black Holes Could Unlock the Mysteries of the Universe – Episode 62 – Behind the Wings – Podcast Episode – Podscan.fm |url=https://podscan.fm/podcasts/behind-the-wings/episodes/how-black-holes-could-unlock-the-mysteries-of-the-universe-episode-62 |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=podscan.fm |language=en}}</ref> He said he commuted home to attend Harvard classes, where he learned Chinese.<ref name=":1" /> He then lived in [[Hong Kong]], where he worked in factories, farms, and wrote for a [[Chinese language]] daily<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nadkarni |first=Vithal C. |date=2004-12-10 |title=Hanging by a String: It may all be a single issue, after all |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/hanging-by-a-string-it-may-all-be-a-single-issue-after-all/articleshow/955294.cms?from=mdr |access-date=2025-12-08 |work=The Economic Times |issn=0013-0389}}</ref> until he was 20.<ref name=":1" /> He considered becoming an [[Investigative journalism|investigative journalist]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Communes, Reporting And Solitonic Solutions {{!}} News {{!}} The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1997/10/16/communes-reporting-and-solitonic-solutions-pprofessor/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=www.thecrimson.com}}</ref> Strominger then returned to [[Harvard College]], after he decided he wanted to be a [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]].<ref name=":1" /> He graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] (AB) in Physics in 1977.<ref name=":0" />

After receiving his AB, Strominger was advised to go enter a [[postgraduate education]] program at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where there were several [[Nobel laureates]] at the time. He said that his advisors discouraged him from continuing in the field,<ref name=":1" /> so after receiving his [[Master of Arts]] in 1979,<ref name=":0" /> he pursued a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (PhD) at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT).<ref name=":1" /> He graduated in 1982.<ref name=":0" />

== Research and career ==
In 1982, Strominger joined the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] as a visiting scholar.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-12-09 |title=Andrew Strominger – Scholars – Institute for Advanced Study |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/andrew-strominger |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=www.ias.edu |language=en}}</ref> While at MIT, he began working on [[quantum gravity]] alongside his thesis work on [[quantum chromodynamics]] and [[Yang–Mills theory]]. At the IAS, he sought to approach quantum gravity from the geometric perspective of [[general relativity]], as opposed to [[string theory]]-based approaches inspired by [[particle physics]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1985 he co-discovered [[Calabi–Yau manifold]] compactifications,<ref name=":2" /> showing that a [[superstring theory]] could simultaneously incorporate gravity and all known particle types and suggesting that it could unify the fundamental laws of physics.<ref name=":3">{{Citation |last=Polchinski |first=Joseph |title=String theory. 2: Superstring theory and beyond |date=2005 |access-date= |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-63304-8}}</ref> This was considered to be a seminal paper of string theory.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Nadis |first=Steve |date=June 13, 2016 |title=The Fall and Rise of String Theory |url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-fall-and-rise-of-string-theory-1774 |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Discover Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

Strominger was then offered a [[professorship]] at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], where he had relocated to for the founding of the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in 1979.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=What is the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics? {{!}} KITP |url=https://www.kitp.ucsb.edu/kitp-explained |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=www.kitp.ucsb.edu}}</ref> He joined the faculty in 1986.<ref name=":0" /> There, he co-developed the [[CGHS model]],<ref>{{Cite book |author=Andrew Strominger |title=Lectures on the Infrared Structure of Gravity and Gauge Theory |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2018 |pages=1–3}}</ref> and in 1991, Strominger co-discovered [[Brane|brane solutions]] of string theory,<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> This work was the basis for his 1996 collaboration with [[Cumrun Vafa]], which used [[M-theory]] to provide the first microscopic derivation of [[Black hole thermodynamics|black hole entropy]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Strominger |first1=Andrew |last2=Vafa |first2=Cumrun |date=1996 |title=Microscopic origin of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=379 |issue=1–4 |pages=99–104 |arxiv=hep-th/9601029 |bibcode=1996PhLB..379...99S |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(96)00345-0}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Howlett |first=Joseph |date=2024-09-25 |title=The #1 Clue to Quantum Gravity Sits on the Surfaces of Black Holes |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-1-clue-to-quantum-gravity-sits-on-the-surfaces-of-black-holes-20240925/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref> This result gave a microscopic explanation of how black holes are able to store information and connected string theory, for the first time, to a physical problem.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Johnson |first=George |date=September 22, 1998 |title=Almost in Awe, Physicists Ponder 'Ultimate' Theory |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/library/national/science/092298sci-string.html |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=archive.nytimes.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cole |first=K.C. |date=1999-11-16 |title='M' Theory Stands for Magic, Matrix, Membrane, Mother or Mystery |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-nov-16-mn-34088-story.html |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> The same year, Strominger, [[Shing-Tung Yau]], and [[Eric Zaslow]] introduced the [[SYZ conjecture]] as a precise formulation of [[mirror symmetry]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hartnett |first=Kevin |date=2018-04-09 |title=Mathematicians Explore Mirror Link Between Two Geometric Worlds |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-explore-mirror-link-between-two-geometric-worlds-20180409/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

In 1997, Strominger joined Harvard as the director of the [[Center for the Fundamental Laws of Nature]].<ref name=":0" /> In 2001, he introduced the [[dS/CFT correspondence]], a version of the [[AdS/CFT correspondence|AdS/CFT]] adapted to [[de Sitter space]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Strominger |first=Andrew |date=2001-10-26 |title=The dS/CFT correspondence |url=http://stacks.iop.org/1126-6708/2001/i=10/a=034?key=crossref.120bc26b29ed6bb5d6b5a4cd98abc7dc |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |volume=2001 |issue=10 |pages=034–034 |doi=10.1088/1126-6708/2001/10/034 |issn=1029-8479|arxiv=hep-th/0106113 }}</ref> suggesting that techniques from [[holography]] could be extended beyond [[anti-de Sitter space]] to more realistic cosmological settings.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Castro |first=Alejandra |last2=Maloney |first2=Alexander |last3=Strominger |first3=Andrew |date=2010-07-13 |title=Hidden conformal symmetry of the Kerr black hole |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.82.024008 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=82 |issue=2 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.82.024008 |issn=1550-7998|arxiv=1004.0996 }}</ref> Two years later in 2003, Strominger had associate with [[Jeffrey Epstein]] who gave a cheque of $100,000 to the [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]], Strominger had facilitated this gift.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=December 9, 2003 |title=Endowment reward for string theorists |url=https://cerncourier.com/a/endowment-reward-for-string-theorists/ |work= |location= |publisher=CERN |access-date=7 May 2026}}</ref> In 2009, Strominger and collaborators developed the [[Kerr/CFT correspondence]] using ideas from AdS/CFT, which describes extremal [[Kerr metric|Kerr black holes]] by a dual description in terms of a conformal field theory.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Guica |first=Monica |last2=Hartman |first2=Thomas |last3=Song |first3=Wei |last4=Strominger |first4=Andrew |date=2009-12-07 |title=The Kerr/CFT correspondence |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.80.124008 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=80 |issue=12 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.80.124008 |issn=1550-7998|arxiv=0809.4266 }}</ref>

In 2016, Strominger, [[Stephen Hawking]], and [[Malcolm Perry (physicist)|Malcolm Perry]] introduced the idea of [[soft hair (black holes)|soft hair on black holes]] as a potential way to resolve the [[black hole information paradox]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Isaacs-Thomas |first=Bella |date=2019-12-27 |title=3 major moments from the ‘golden’ decade of black holes |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/3-major-moments-from-the-golden-decade-of-black-holes |access-date=2025-12-09 |website=PBS News |language=en-us}}</ref> Also in 2016, Strominger and his student [[Sabrina Pasterski]] discovered a novel spin memory affect, involving a connection which Pasterski found between symmetries and a spin that can be observed in [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=McCormick |first=Katie |date=2021-12-08 |title=Gravitational Waves Should Permanently Distort Space-Time |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/gravitational-waves-should-permanently-distort-space-time-20211208/ |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pasterski |first1=Sabrina |last2=Strominger |first2=Andrew |last3=Zhiboedov |first3=Alexander |date=14 December 2016 |title=New gravitational memories |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |volume=2016 |issue=12 |pages=53 |arxiv=1502.06120 |bibcode=2016JHEP...12..053P |doi=10.1007/JHEP12(2016)053 |s2cid=256045385}}</ref>

In 2020, Strominger outlined a program to use the infrared triangle,<ref name=":1" /> an equivalence he developed between soft theorems in [[quantum field theory]],<ref name=":9" >{{Cite web |last=Beall |first=Abigail |date=August 2, 2023 |title=Does space-time remember? The search for gravitational memory |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg25934501-400-does-space-time-remember-the-search-for-gravitational-memory/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Gravitational memory effect|gravitational memory effects]], and the [[Bondi–Metzner–Sachs group]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Strominger |first=Andrew |title=Lectures on the Infrared Structure of Gravity and Gauge Theory |date=2018 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-17973-5 |location=Princeton}}</ref> to extend the [[holographic principle]] to the [[flat space]] geometry of the universe, beyond anti-de Sitter space.<ref name=":1" /> He and his colleagues then developed the subfield of [[celestial holography]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=FirstPrinciples |date=2024-08-08 |title=Andrew Strominger: Pioneering Celestial Holography |url=https://www.firstprinciples.org/article/andrew-strominger-loves-string-theory-but-is-ready-to-be-in-the-real-world |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=FirstPrinciples |language=en}}</ref> He emphasized the bottom-up nature of the framework, which provides falsifiability through the potential for observation and testable frameworks, particularly by gravitational wave detectors like [[LIGO]] or [[Laser Interferometer Space Antenna|LISA]].<ref name=":7" /> In 2021, Strominger and his colleagues derived the symmetry algebra governing celestial [[Conformal field theory|conformal field theories]], showing that the symmetry structure expected on the [[celestial sphere]] matches a well studied algebra that appears in string theory and condensed matter systems, thereby placing strong constraints on the possible form of a flat space [[Holographic duality|holographic dual]].<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=McCormick |first=Katie |date=2022-01-12 |title=Symmetries Reveal Clues About the Holographic Universe |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/symmetries-reveal-clues-about-the-holographic-universe-20220112/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

Strominger is the collaboration director and a [[principal investigator]] of the [[Simons Foundation]] Collaboration on Celestial Holography.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Simons Collaboration on Celestial Holography {{!}} Department of Physics |url=https://www.physics.harvard.edu/SCCH |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=www.physics.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-10 |title=People |url=https://simonscelestialholographycollaboration.org/people/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Simons Collaboration on Celestial Holography |language=en-US}}</ref> He is considered a pioneer of the subfield.<ref name=":7" />

== Awards and honors ==

* Fellow, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], 2001<ref name=":0" />
* [[Leonard Eisenbud]] Prize, [[American Mathematical Society]], 2008<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2008 |title=2008 Eisenbud Prize |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200804/tx080400505p.pdf |website=American Mathematical Society}}</ref>
* [[Oskar Klein Medal]], [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]], 2014<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-11-14 |title=Andy Strominger Awarded 2014 Oskar Klein Medal {{!}} Center for the Fundamental Laws of Nature |url=https://hetg.physics.harvard.edu/news/proessor-strominger-awarded-2014-oskar-klein-medal |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=hetg.physics.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]], [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]], 2014<ref>{{Cite web |title=ICTP Announces 2014 Dirac Medallists {{!}} ICTP |url=https://www.ictp.it/news/2014/8/ictp-announces-2014-dirac-medallists |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=www.ictp.it}}</ref>
* [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]], [[American Physical Society]], 2016<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-01 |title=Andrew Strominger awarded 2016 Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics from American Physical Society {{!}} Center for the Fundamental Laws of Nature |url=https://hetg.physics.harvard.edu/news/andrew-strominger-awarded-2016-dannie-heineman-prize-mathematical-physics-american |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=hetg.physics.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref>
* [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]], 2017<ref>{{Cite web |title=Breakthrough Prize – Fundamental Physics Breakthrough Prize Laureates – Andrew Strominger |url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/1/L3796 |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=breakthroughprize.org |language=en}}</ref>
* Fellow, [[American Physical Society]], 2018<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Fellows Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship |website=American Physical Society}}</ref>
* Fellow, [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]], 2020<ref>{{Cite news |title=Andrew Strominger – John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/andrew-strominger/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221124101623/https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/andrew-strominger/ |archive-date=2022-11-24 |access-date=2025-12-08 |work=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref>
